Ocean sunfish (Mola mola) hatch from pelagic eggs as minuscule larvae, with the newly emerged yolk-sac larva measuring just 0.25 centimeters [Lb = 0.25 centimeters] in total length at birth. This extraordinarily small size at hatching, among the smallest of any teleost relative to adult dimensions, marks the beginning of a growth trajectory that is virtually unparalleled among bony fishes. Following eclosion, the lecithotrophic larva undergoes rapid development, transitioning to exogenous feeding within a matter of days. The initial body mass of these hatchlings, derived from an egg diameter of approximately 1.3 millimeters, is estimated at 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams] of wet weight at birth. This remarkably low birth mass—barely more than a milligram—contrasts starkly with the colossal size the species eventually achieves. Field surveys and captive observations have documented that individuals can attain an ultimate total length of 270 centimeters [Li = 270 centimeters], measured from the mouth to the tail. This impressive maximum length, among the largest of all extant bony fishes, is accompanied by an equally staggering ultimate wet weight of 2,300,000 grams [Wwi = 2,300,000 grams], a figure recorded from a specimen landed at Kamogawa, Japan in 1996.

Reproductive biology in Ocean sunfish is characterized by extreme fecundity, an adaptation that compensates for high early-life mortality in the pelagic environment. Puberty, or the onset of gonadal maturation, is estimated to occur when individuals reach approximately 155 centimeters [Lp = approximately 155 centimeters] in total length at puberty, a value derived from comparative studies with related tetraodontiform species. At this size, females are believed to initiate vitellogenesis and become capable of spawning. For an adult female at a typical reproductive length of 137 centimeters, the daily reproductive output at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] is estimated to be approximately 82 million eggs per day . This prodigious rate of gamete release, the highest reported for any vertebrate, reflects a reproductive strategy centered on producing vast numbers of small, pelagic eggs that are broadcast into the water column during spawning events. The sheer numerical output compensates for the negligible survival probability of each individual offspring through the early larval stages.

Growth in Mola mola is remarkably rapid during the first few years of life, a period of intense growth before the individual diverts resources toward reproduction. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a juvenile sunfish that begins its post-settlement life at a mass of roughly 26 kilograms can reach a wet weight of 399,000 grams  after 454 days. This represents an increase in body mass of more than fifteen-fold over approximately fifteen months, a growth rate that is exceptional even among fast-growing pelagic fishes. The thermal regime of 25 °C is crucial for maintaining the high metabolic rates necessary to sustain such rapid tissue accretion; cooler temperatures would substantially slow this growth trajectory. This accelerated growth phase allows the species to quickly pass through size windows of high predation vulnerability, a common selective pressure among large-bodied marine predators. The conversion of ingested gelatinous prey into somatic tissue appears to be highly efficient, fueling this dramatic increase in body mass.

Life history theory for large, slow-maturing marine fishes often predicts extended longevity, and the available data for Mola mola are consistent with this expectation. The maximum lifespan for the species, estimated under the assumption of sustained growth at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is approximately 14,600 days [am = approximately 14,600 days], which corresponds to about 40 years. This estimate of four decades is conservative, as some individuals in the wild may exceed this benchmark under favorable oceanographic conditions. Such a long lifespan is ecologically significant because it allows for repeated, iteroparous spawning events over many years, a strategy that buffers the population against years of poor recruitment. The large body size achieved by senescent adults, nearing the ultimate total length of 270 centimeters [Li = 270 centimeters] and ultimate wet weight of 2,300,000 grams [Wwi = 2,300,000 grams], likely reduces natural mortality from predation, allowing these aging individuals to persist in the ecosystem as dominant consumers of gelatinous zooplankton.

Comparative physiology of Ocean sunfish reveals a suite of adaptations linked to its unusual morphology and pelagic lifestyle. Unlike many fast-swimming scombrids or billfishes, Mola mola lacks a swim bladder and possesses a largely cartilaginous skeleton, yet it achieves a maximum total length of 270 centimeters [Li = 270 centimeters]. The species is commonly observed basking at the sea surface, a behavior thought to facilitate thermoregulation after deep foraging dives into cooler waters. While the primary spawning rate is tied to a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the fish can tolerate a wide thermal range during its daily vertical migrations. The extreme fecundity, with a potential daily output of millions of eggs at size 137 centimeters  when maintained at 25 °C, remains a subject of intense study. The contrast between the diminutive 0.0012 gram [Wwb = 0.0012 gram] birth mass and the adult mass exceeding two tons underscores one of the most dramatic ontogenetic size increases in the animal kingdom.
